channel.title: Nature Climate Change
channel.description: Nature Climate Change is a monthly journal dedicated to publishing high-quality research papers that describe the most significant and cutting-edge research on the causes, impacts and wider implications of global climate change. The journal publishes climate research across the physical, biological and social sciences and strives to integrate and communicate interdisciplinary research. The journal aims to play a leading role in: providing accessibility to a broad audience to research published both within and outside the journal; raising the visibility of climate change research in related research communities as well as the mainstream media; and offering a forum for discussion of the challenges faced by researchers and policy makers (and other interested parties) in understanding the complex mechanisms and impacts associated with the Earth’s changing climate.

item.title: Brazil’s data-driven plan for climate-resilient healthcare
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02779-7

By integrating climate risk into health planning, Brazil is redesigning healthcare to withstand floods, heatwaves and other climate shocks.
item.dc:title: Brazil’s data-driven plan for climate-resilient healthcare
item.dc:creator: Lisa Palmer
item.dc:source: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 2026-11-03; | doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02779-7

item.title: Time to drop the no-policy business-as-usual baselines
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02787-7

Baseline construction shapes estimates of mitigation cost, ambition and progress, while no-policy counterfactuals could vary with choices about policy, technology and development. Rather than relying on one constructed baseline, assessments and related conclusions should be compared across plausible baselines.
item.dc:title: Time to drop the no-policy business-as-usual baselines
item.dc:creator: Mel George
Anand Patwardhan
item.dc:source: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 2026-11-03; | doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02787-7

item.title: Zero emissions commitment depends on warming level
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 03 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02776-w

The global temperature change that happens after emissions cease is expected to be close to zero. Here the authors use model simulations to show that this zero emissions commitment depends on the warming level at which emissions cease and might be positive for higher warming.

item.title: Southeast Asian voices on climate change
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 02 November 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02783-x

Responding to the increasing risks of climate change in Southeast Asia requires research and effective action that considers the unique challenges of the region. In this Viewpoint, researchers and practitioners from the region share their views on the progress made in understanding and responding to climate change.

item.title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 30 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x

The long-term response of the Greenland and Antarctic ice sheets to warming is often studied using ice-only simulations. Here the authors use a coupled ice–atmosphere–ocean model and find that East Antarctica remains stable even under higher warming because changes in atmospheric circulation increase precipitation sensitivity.
item.dc:title: Atmospheric stabilization of the East Antarctic ice sheet under warming
item.dc:creator: Kyung-Sook Yun
Axel Timmermann
item.dc:source: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 2026-10-30; | doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02791-x

item.title: Closing the climate–economics communication gap
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02784-w

As the IPCC is in its seventh assessment cycle, bridging the gap between physical climate science and economics has become more urgent. Estimating climate damages requires a rigorous translation of physical hazards into economic losses, highlighting the need for better communication between the disciplines.
item.dc:title: Closing the climate–economics communication gap

item.title: Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 28 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

This work investigates the effect of the 2016 regime shift in Antarctic sea ice on Antarctic Intermediate Water (AAIW). The authors show that decreased sea ice and reduced freshwater subduction lead to saltier and denser AAIW, with implications for wide-scale water-mass properties.
item.dc:title: Reversal of Antarctic Intermediate Water trends triggered by sea ice decline
item.dc:creator: Kaushik Mishra
Bishakhdatta Gayen
Alberto C. Naveira Garabato
item.dc:source: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 2026-10-28; | doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02758-y

item.title: Climate warming boosts frequency and intensity of southern Africa’s rainfall extremes
item.content:encoded:
Nature Climate Change, Published online: 23 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02772-0

Extreme southward swings of the South Indian convergence zone (a major source of rainfall across southern Africa) can trigger devastating floods. Climate-model projections indicate that these swings might occur twice as often in the twenty-first century as in the previous century and produce more intense rainfall, owing to an increased land–sea temperature contrast and poleward intensification of atmospheric circulation.
item.dc:title: Climate warming boosts frequency and intensity of southern Africa’s rainfall extremes
item.dc:source: Nature Climate Change, Published online: 2026-10-23; | doi:10.1038/s41558-026-02772-0
